title: Fine-Tuning at Home: Beat Frontier Models With 8 Steps
description: A two-host walkthrough of a knowledge graph built from Maxime Rivest's article "Even you can now fine-tune an LLM, and maybe you finally should." The claim: with a coding agent, a frontier "teacher" model and LoRA adapters on consumer hardware, fine-tuning a task-specific model is now something one person can do. Covers the eight-step workflow, synthetic distillation, why training loss kept improving while rubric scores plateaued, the roughly 1,000-example saturation point, the break-even math (about 170 papers per hour), licensing limits on training with model outputs, and the last-mile accuracy problem. Benchmark figures are the author's own reported results.

title: Super Is Not Superior
description: A deep dive into Tejas Kumar's essay "AI Is Now SI: Super Intelligence Isn't Superior," via a knowledge graph of its argument. The essay says "super" describes task performance while "superior" claims worth, and that renaming AI "Super Intelligence" blurs the two. Covers Bostrom's definition of superintelligence, real machine milestones, the BCG "jagged frontier" study, the golden calf, Calvin's "forge of idols," the sun renamed "the greater light" in Genesis, and the essay's case for loyalty as a willingness to overpay. 2026 events are as reported in the essay.

title: When Your GTM Brain Lives in Git
description: A two-host walkthrough of a knowledge graph built from John Kutay's post "GTM in git," based on his San Francisco talk "Your GTM Belongs in git." The argument: put as much go-to-market work as possible into a git repo that coding agents can reason over, test and scale, with the repo as the "logical brain" and hosted infrastructure taking over only when scale demands it. Covers Rippling's GrowthOS (usage figures are self-reported), agent harnesses and sandboxes, GTM evals, context engineering and shared definitions, and the marketer-as-AI-engineer shift. Also the graph's own additions: a GitOps lineage, a governance caution about agents querying production data, and why "ideas become the bottleneck" is still a contested prediction.

title: The Slop Superhighway
description: Rhys Sullivan argues that agents flooding human channels like GitHub issues isn't the real failure. The failure is that there's no agent-to-agent channel to carry that traffic, so humans end up as 'meat proxies' copy-pasting between AIs. We walk through his first-person Cloudflare bug story (single-sourced), the 2025 issueslop backlash, what exists today (author-side issue triage, MCP, A2A), and what's still missing: identity, payments, and defenses against prompt injection. We close with economics and liability lenses, which the knowledge graph adds as its own speculative extensions rather than claims from the post.

title: How to Research Anything
description: A walk through Polymath Investor's practitioner guide to independent research: scope a small question that passes the 'So what?' test, cap your time, skim twenty sources and read three deeply, check key facts against three independent witnesses, and decide what 'done' means before you start. The knowledge graph adds its own theory lenses, flagged as interpretation, most notably that the guide's 'plateau of diminishing returns' mirrors the foraging rule ecologists use for when an animal should move on. We also cover the tensions the graph raises and the guide leaves unaddressed: AI summaries may erode the outsider's fresh eyes, and expert calls aren't independent witnesses. The guide is one person's advice, not a tested method, and its paywalled section is known only from a teaser.

title: How to Research Anything, Part 1: The Method
description: Part 1 of a two-parter on Polymath Investor's practitioner guide to independent research. We walk one made-up project through the whole method: scope a small question that passes the 'So what?' test, cap your time, choose sources that will still matter in a year, skim twenty and read three deeply, check key facts against three independent witnesses, keep one-idea notes with their sources, and decide what 'done' means before you start. The guide is one person's untested advice, and its paywalled section is known only from a teaser. Ends with a teaser for Part 2.

title: How to Research Anything, Part 2: Why It Works
description: Part 2 opens with a quick recap of the method, then looks at why it might work and where it falls short. The knowledge graph adds outside theories, all flagged as interpretation: the guide's 'plateau of diminishing returns' mirrors ecology's rule for when a forager should leave a patch, 'useful a year from now?' estimates how fast a field's facts go stale, and a pre-set 'done' is Herbert Simon's satisficing. Then two tensions the guide leaves unaddressed: AI summaries may erode the outsider's fresh eyes, and expert calls aren't independent witnesses. We close with cross-domain synthesis and the author's compounding research playbook.

title: Cancer's Second Verb: Converting Tumors Instead of Killing Them
description: A walk through a knowledge graph built from Brian Roemmele's X post on a KAIST study (Advanced Science, 2024). As the post tells it, researchers built a 'digital twin' of an intestinal cell's gene network, used an algorithm called BENEIN to pick three genes (MYB, HDAC2, FOXA2), and turned colon cancer cells into normal-like cells in cell lines and mice by maturing them rather than killing them. This is early preclinical work with no human data, described secondhand, and nothing here is medical advice. The graph adds context: differentiation therapy has treated the leukemia APL for decades, the idea builds on Waddington, Kauffman and Yamanaka, and hard-to-drug targets, durability (speculative) and the tumor's surroundings could keep it from becoming a therapy.

title: Prediction Markets, Part 1: How a Price Becomes a Forecast
description: Part 1 of a two-parter built from a knowledge graph on prediction markets. A contract pays one dollar if an event happens, so its price reads as a probability. We cover why economists think that should work (Hayek's idea that prices pool scattered knowledge, plus Arrow-Debreu and efficient markets), the automated market maker that keeps thin markets trading, corporate markets at firms like Google, and how the law shaped the field: Iowa Electronic Markets, Intrade's shutdown, Polymarket's exit and 2025 return, and Kalshi's court win. We end with catastrophe bonds as an older, professional version of the same idea. Dated events were checked against news coverage. Not betting or investment advice.

title: Prediction Markets, Part 2: When the Price Lies
description: Part 2 opens with a quick recap, then a March 2025 Polymarket market on a Ukraine minerals deal that, per news reports, resolved 'yes' with no deal signed after a token-holder vote. We cover the favorite-longshot bias (prices act like betting odds in the tails), wash trading and why volume isn't proof (estimates vary widely), oracles as the real point of centralization, and the parallel with catastrophe-bond triggers. Then the rivals: the Good Judgment Project's superforecasters and no-money platforms like Metaculus and Manifold, where the comparisons are messy. We close with futarchy, Hanson's untested idea to 'vote on values, bet on beliefs.' Not betting or investment advice.

title: References, Part 1: The Police Sketch
description: How Brett Berson's composite referencing works: references as a police sketch built from many witnesses, front-door and back-door calls, the whose-side-are-they-on check, story-and-comparison questions, the 12/5/3 call counts, running references early because of confirmation bias, and how to judge the person giving the reference.

title: References, Part 2: Marriage After a Second Date
description: Why Berson's reference method works and where it falls short: hiring as marriage after a second date, context-dependent performance, the hardwired-traits debate and selection research, legal limits on what references say, AI-summarized reference calls, two-way due diligence, and the method's roots in Graham Duncan's essay.

title: Spotting Weakness in Seconds: Prison Eyes and Miami Doors
description: A deep dive into a viral post claiming inmates can spot a 'weak man' in seconds: the 1981 and 2013 victim-selection studies behind it, thin-slicing and psychopathy, the leap to Miami's velvet ropes and the walled-garden roots of 'paradise', and how the post's wolves-and-sheep rhetoric doubles as its paywall pitch.

title: Hiring in the Age of AI, Part 1: What Survived the Interview Lab
description: JD Pruett's 20/10 philosophy: when coding agents eat the middle 70% of a project, hire for the first 20% (framing, architecture, taste) and the last 10% (shipping). We walk through the interview formats he tried and dropped — the agent-assisted long onsite, the AI systems design round, rule-of-thumb trivia — and the two that survived: unassisted code review with 'what if' changes, and an onsite that opens with a market presentation and then three shrinking timed problems, all judged by whether interviewers can give a confident thumbs up or down.

title: Hiring in the Age of AI, Part 2: Judging Depth You Can't Check
description: How do you judge a candidate whose field you don't know? Pruett's rules of thumb: deep versus shallow simplicity, speed under pressure, a walk-through of a problem from 18+ months ago, and telling people who recognize the underlying problem from people who match on surface labels — backed by the 1981 Chi, Feltovich and Glaser physics-sorting study, and the idea that agent 'memory' is really cache invalidation. Then the pushback: trading standardization for interviewer confidence, and a speculative worry about where junior engineers get their reps.

title: The New Manager, Part 1: You Are the Weather
description: Louise Deason's 'Ten things nobody tells you when you become a manager', things one to five: your output is the team's output, stop doing the work and hand over outcomes, touch nothing for the first few weeks, you are the weather, and let your reports run the one-on-one. Plus context the source map adds, not Deason: the Peter Principle, the Theory of Constraints, Chesterton's fence, and why a leader's idle remark lands as an order.

title: The New Manager, Part 2: The Seat You Took
description: Things six to ten from Louise Deason's essay: absorb the mess from above and argue it upstairs, manage your own manager, give hard feedback early and kindly, keep receipts so you can fight for people in rooms they're not in, and know that management is no longer a safe seat. Plus the source map's own additions: emotional labor, psychological safety, the 'unbossing' squeeze on middle managers (including a reported Gartner forecast), and the algorithmic boss.

title: The New CFO, Part 1: From Scorekeeper to Builder
description: Seema Amble's a16z essay argues AI is rewriting the CFO job: from producing numbers to designing the company's operating system. We cover the four CFO eras, how cheap data turns the finance stack into a teammate, skills maintained like code, the zero-day close, agents and compute on the P&L, and why controls are what make speed safe. Company examples are attributed, not verified.

title: The New CFO, Part 2: The Finance Engineer
description: The people side of Seema Amble's 'You Need a New CFO': the finance engineer, vibecoding, teams shrinking from about 5% of headcount toward 2%, why senior experts like the head of tax gain most from AI, and 'walk me through your prompt sequence.' Plus three ideas the knowledge map adds on top of the essay, including a speculative worry about the career ladder.

title: The Software Foreman, Part 1: Attention, Not Code
description: Stephen Margheim argues AI in software is optimizing the wrong thing: his team's bottleneck isn't writing code, it's attention. We cover the software factory vs the software foreman, a bug that broke links only for unused accounts and was found by luck, Claude debugging it from a single message link, and the data lake and query-based watches that give attention a place to look.

title: The Software Foreman, Part 2: Watch Everything, Interrupt Rarely
description: How Margheim's software foreman thinks: notice, hypothesize, check, then drop it or escalate with evidence. Plus persistent background agents, his 'noise beats silence' stance, the crying-wolf risk, and the ten-minute human review. Then four ideas the knowledge map adds on its own: control charts, Toyota's gemba walk, Herbert Simon on attention, and the METR study where developers felt faster but were slower.

title: The Night AI Emptied Math's Open Problems, Part 1: Scooped
description: A Proofs and Prompts post collects 100+ mathematicians' reactions to OpenAI's reported October 6 release of hundreds of claimed solutions to open problems. Part 1 covers the event, proofs arriving faster than anyone can read them, withdrawals and partial formal checks, Peter Scholze's cryptography worry, a declined advisory recommendation, and three hard-hit voices: Wilton, Zaremsky and Duminil-Copin. Counts and verification status are as reported in the post, not independently confirmed.

title: The Night AI Emptied Math's Open Problems, Part 2: Grieving and Thrilled
description: The human side of mathematicians' reactions to the AI math release: PhD students and postdocs facing scooped theses, Tasmin Chu's grant and security worries, Cyril Houdayer's genuine thrill, Terence Tao on losing the first encounter with a problem, the unpaid work of reading and explaining the proofs, Danny Calegari's zippers, and a thread of Dolly Parton, Solaris and E. E. Cummings.

title: The AI Value Creation Problem, Part 1: Two of Three Levers
description: Mark Ajzenstadt argues private equity AI plans collapse into headcount cuts because they fit the earnings bridge, while returns come from three levers: earnings growth, the exit multiple and time. We walk through his illustrative math where one point of multiple erases 60% of the equity gain, Bain's tougher return arithmetic, and the diligence question he expects next. The author discloses a commercial interest; cited reports are as summarized in his essay.

title: The AI Value Creation Problem, Part 2: Proprietary Observation
description: Why the people a payroll spreadsheet marks as savings may hold a company's real AI advantage: Box and Ramp data on AI leaders growing headcount, Gartner's rehiring forecast, 'proprietary observation beats proprietary data,' fieldwork, release quality, a vendor case study we treat as illustration only, and portfolio reuse, plus a fund-fee incentive the knowledge map adds.

title: How Stories Create Alignment, Part 1: The Story as Operating System
description: Hiten Shah argues a company runs on one shared story: held in the same words by every team, owned and retold by the founder, and used as a yes-or-no filter for decisions. We cover his five ideas, then the research the knowledge map adds (not cited by Shah) to explain why it might work: Fisher's narrative paradigm, narrative transportation and neural coupling, shared mental models, Weick, Schein and Rumelt.

title: How Stories Create Alignment, Part 2: When the Story Goes Wrong
description: Beyond Hiten Shah's essay, entirely the knowledge map's additions: Shiller's narrative economics, category design and stories as replicators, then two failure modes Shah doesn't address, narrative lock-in and the map's own speculative idea of 'narrative debt', plus speculative takes on the story as lossy compression and AI agents that retell or counterfeit a founder's story.
